html:
The Bamum script is a writing system for the Bamum language of western Cameroon, created by King Ibrahim Njoya of Bamum from 1896. Over fourteen years he and his helpers reshaped it six times, from a set of several hundred picture signs into a lean syllabary of about eighty signs.

Njoya ruled the kingdom from his capital, Foumban. He was curious about writing he had seen in Arabic and German, and wanted his people to have their own. With the script his court wrote down the history and customs of Bamum, medical recipes, maps and laws. He set up schools to teach it, and in 1918 metal type was cast for printing.

Njoya dealt shrewdly first with the Germans of Kamerun and then with the French of French Cameroons, but the French saw him as a rival. They cut his power, closed his schools and exiled him in 1931, and the script fell out of use. A revival began in the 2000s, and the script is now in the Unicode standard. It stands beside the Vai syllabary and N'Ko as one of the African scripts invented in modern times.
